extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, and legal scholars litigating or studying unfair competition and property rights in news/market information
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-analytic standards for when appropriation or copying of news/market information constitutes unfair competition and justifies injunctions. Focused on factual tests, precedent-based principles, and statutory (FTC Act §5) remedies in the news-collection/distribution business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of dedication (public performance vs. abandonment of rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: The owner's rights are lost only to the extent of any dedication; public performance of a work does not necessarily constitute a dedication permitting reproduction or competitive use. 'It is not that the spectator learns the whole play which entitles the author to object; it is the use that is sought to be made of that which is learned which affords just ground of complaint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the proprietor unmistakably intended to abandon rights generally or merely granted a limited use; if dedication is partial, the public acquires rights only to the extent plainly given and any excess use violates reserved rights. (Cites Tompkins v. Halleck and Aronson v. Baker.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Peculiar commercial value of certain works (basis for protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subject matter (e.g., plays for scenic representation; news as a 'business commodity') has a peculiar value beyond mere literary or informational content which justifies special protective treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, recognize and weight non-literary or commercial attributes (scenic value, timeliness, cost of collection/distribution) as part of the proprietary interest deserving protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public delivery/performance does not permit reproduction or republication for competitive use
rubrics_metrics.description: Public exhibition, delivery of lectures (even with printed copies), exhibition of pictures, or publication of engravings were held not to constitute a dedication permitting unauthorized reproduction or redelivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare factual context (e.g., whether copies were provided for students or merely presentation) to precedents (Drummond v. Altenus; Werchmeister v. Am. Lith. Co.; Turner v. Robinson) to determine whether the public's access extends to competitive reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property in news and market information created by collection at expense
rubrics_metrics.description: A company that collects and makes available timely market news or quotations at considerable expense may have a property interest in that information (e.g., Board of Trade v. Christie Grain & Stock Co.; National Telegraph News Co. v. Western Union).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimant's labor, expense, and system for making the information available (speed, distribution network) created an exploitably proprietary asset deserving equitable protection and potential injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlawful appropriation when competitor uses collected news bodily for sale without original effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking complainant's news from early bulletins/editions and distributing/selling it bodily without original investigation or substantial expense is unfair business competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between using others' reports as leads for original investigation (which may be permissible) and wholesale copying/reshuffling of collected material to sell as one's own product; the latter supports injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated unfair methods of competition (specific actionable acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: By especially the following methods the defendant may be restrained: (1) bribing or inducing custodians of complainant's news to reveal it; (2) causing members to violate contracts/confidential relations; (3) appropriating news collected at complainant's expense and selling it exploiting time differences and telegraphic speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When alleging unfair competition, plead and prove specific methods (bribery, inducing breaches, systematic appropriation) as independent grounds for equitable relief, supported by affidavits and documentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition method immaterial if the use is unfair
rubrics_metrics.description: It is immaterial whether the defendant acquired the news by stealing, bribing, inducing breaches, reading from machines, voluntary revelation, or taking from bulletins — if the use competes unfairly and deprives complainant of its fruits, injunction is warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus inquiry on the defendant's use and effect (does it obtain fruits of another's labor free?) rather than on the technical legality of the acquisition alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying per se is not unlawful; context and purpose determine unlawfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying news is not unlawful in and of itself; it becomes unlawful when done systematically as a business method to acquire another's labor and expenditure free of cost and to deprive the originator of the fruits of its industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intent, systematic practice, effect on the producer's ability to recoup costs, and whether copying supplants the producer's market; mere incidental copying for ordinary public uses is distinguishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part equitable test: fairness between parties and public interest in business efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider (1) fairness as between parties — no one should compete against a rival 'out of the rival's own pocket' — and (2) the public interest in the efficiency of business as the public's means of supporting life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both private fairness (misappropriation of rival's investment) and broader public policy (whether the practice would undermine sustainable news collection/distribution) in deciding relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts lawful in isolation may be unlawful as part of a scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: No act is 'unlawful per se'; otherwise-innocent acts may become unlawful if they are steps in an overall scheme to restrain trade or engage in unfair competition (Holmes, Aikens v. Wisconsin, Swift & Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at the aggregate plan, purpose, and cumulative effect of conduct rather than treating each act in isolation when assessing legality under unfair competition principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malicious purpose to destroy competitor can render otherwise permissible conduct unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: If a defendant's real motive is malicious — e.g., to drive a rival out of business by subsidized competition or sham operations — otherwise permissible acts (opening competing shops, selling below cost) may be enjoined (Tuttle v. Buck; Dunshee v. Standard Oil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence of intent, funding, temporary strategies, or subsidization aimed at elimination of a competitor; such proof supports equitable relief even where individual acts are typically lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent protection of collected information and rapid dissemination as property
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have protected exchanges' and telegraph companies' quotations and news when dissemination speed and method constituted the company's valuable property right (Board of Trade, Hunt v. New York Cotton Exchange, National Telegraph News Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing protection, cite analogous precedents showing recognition of proprietary rights in timely, collected information and demonstrate comparable factual structures (expense, exclusivity of distribution, customer reliance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation of values created by competitor's expenditures (subtle forms of unfair competition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtle form of competition involves appropriating values created by a competitor's expenditures (e.g., taking information collected for sale at large expense and disposing of it in competition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimants should articulate how defendant's conduct leverages claimant's pioneering investments, citing the Bureau of Corporations' 'Trust Laws and Unfair Competition' analysis; courts may be protective even where limits of the doctrine are not fully defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific categories of unfair practices courts have enjoined
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples treated as unfair competition include 'bogus independents', exclusive dealing contracts, 'tying' clauses, preferential rebates to disadvantage rivals, discriminatory/local price reductions to drive out competitors, and 'fighting ship' practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories as analogues when demonstrating that challenged conduct is a recognized form of unfair competition; show functional equivalence if facts do not match precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: True statements and free speech can be unlawful if used to injure in competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absolutely true statements or acts of free speech (e.g., circulating lists saying 'We do not patronize') can be unlawful when used as devices to injure competitors or to effect unfair exclusion (Eastern States Retail Lumber Dealers' Association; Gompers v. Bucks Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate motive, context, and competitive effect of truthful communications; constitutional protection does not automatically immunize statements used as unfair competitive devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis for injunctions against unfair methods: FTC Act §5
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act declares 'unfair methods of competition in commerce' unlawful and supplies a statutory ground for injunctive relief against unfair competitive practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking remedies, plead statutory §5 claims in addition to common-law unfair-competition theories where appropriate; show how defendant's methods fall within 'unfair methods of competition.'
